Equivalence Test for the Population RMSEA (Test of Not Close Fit)

Source: R/equivalence_rmsea.R
equivalence_rmsea.Rd

Tests whether the population root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) of a structural equation model is below a bound the researcher chooses in advance, so that a model can be endorsed as fitting within a stated tolerance rather than merely not rejected. This is the test of not close fit of MacCallum, Browne, and Sugawara (1996), which Yuan, Chan, Marcoulides, and Bentler (2016) present as an equivalence test: the null hypothesis \(H_0: \epsilon \ge \epsilon_0\) that the population RMSEA \(\epsilon\) is at least the bound \(\epsilon_0\) is tested against \(H_1: \epsilon < \epsilon_0\), and rejecting it supports fit within the bound. It reverses the test of close fit (Browne & Cudeck, 1993), whose null hypothesis \(\epsilon \le \epsilon_0\) a well-fitting model merely fails to reject. The function works from the summary statistics a paper reports.

Usage

equivalence_rmsea(
  chisq,
  df,
  N,
  rmsea_bound,
  n_groups = 1,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  sample_size_convention = c("N-1", "N")
)

Arguments

chisq

The model's chi square test statistic \(T\), the likelihood ratio statistic of a normal theory maximum likelihood fit.

df

The model's degrees of freedom, a positive whole number.

N

The total sample size, summed over groups: a whole number greater than n_groups.

rmsea_bound

The bound \(\epsilon_0\): the largest population RMSEA the researcher is prepared to call fit within tolerance, chosen before seeing the data. No universal value is assumed.

n_groups

The number of independent groups of a multiple group model, whose chisq, df, and N are totals over the groups. Default 1.

alpha_level

The one-sided Type I error rate, in \((0, 0.5)\); default 0.05. The interval reported has confidence level \(1 - 2\alpha\), 90 percent at the default.

sample_size_convention

The multiplier \(a\) in \(T = a\hat{F}\) with which chisq was formed: "N-1" (the default), each group's sample size less one, so \(a = N - G\) for \(G\) groups, or "N", so \(a = N\). lavaan's default normal likelihood and Mplus form \(T\) with \(N\), so their statistics take "N".

Value

A dmar_tbl (class dmar_sem_fit) with columns term and value and the rows rmsea (the point estimate \(\sqrt{G \max(T - df, 0)/(a \cdot df)}\)), ci_lower and ci_upper (the \(100(1 - 2\alpha)\) percent interval for the population RMSEA), rmsea_bound, null_noncentrality, p_value, equivalent (1 when the test rejects \(H_0\) at alpha_level, 0 otherwise), chi_square, df, N, and n_groups. The conf_level attribute is \(1 - 2\alpha\). The verdict attribute states the inference in a sentence, and the sem_fit attribute records the sample size convention and multiplier, the boundary convention that applied, and the lines of the printed footer.

Details

Write \(T\) for the chi square statistic on \(df\) degrees of freedom and \(a\) for the multiplier with which it was formed. Under a model whose misfit is small relative to sampling error, \(T\) is approximately noncentral chi square with noncentrality \(\lambda = a \cdot df \cdot \epsilon^2 / G\) (Steiger & Lind, 1980; Browne & Cudeck, 1993; Steiger, 1998, for \(G\) groups). At the boundary of the null hypothesis the noncentrality is \(\lambda_0 = a \cdot df \cdot \epsilon_0^2 / G\) (row null_noncentrality), and a small \(T\) is evidence against \(H_0\), so the p-value is the lower tail, \(P\{\chi^2_{df}(\lambda_0) \le T\}\) (MacCallum et al., 1996, Figure 2). The model is declared within tolerance (row equivalent equal to 1) when the p-value is below alpha_level. The p-value and the interval stay accurate for a statistic in the millions, where R's pchisq() fails (see ci_nc_chisq).

The decision is the same as comparing an interval with the bound. The interval reported is the two-sided \(100(1 - 2\alpha)\) percent interval for the population RMSEA, 90 percent at the default, whose upper limit is the one-sided \(100(1 - \alpha)\) percent upper bound; the p-value is below \(\alpha\) exactly when the upper limit is below \(\epsilon_0\) (MacCallum et al., 1996, Table 1). This is why the RMSEA is conventionally reported with a 90 percent interval (Browne & Cudeck, 1993): its upper limit settles the test of not close fit at level .05 and its lower limit the test of close fit. The upper limit is the T-size RMSEA of Yuan et al. (2016, Eq. 4): the data endorse the model at level \(\alpha\) for every bound above it, so it is the quantity to report when no bound was fixed in advance. The point estimate is truncated at zero; Steiger (2000) shows that the truncation follows from a basic property of a good estimator and costs little in practice, and the interval carries the information about precision. Yuan et al. use \(a = N - 1\), the default here. The function does not compute their T-size CFI (their Eqs. 6 to 10, which divide \(\alpha\) between the model and baseline statistics) or the adjusted cutoff values for judging a T-size index, which their Tables 1 and 2 give as regression coefficients in \(N\) and \(df\)).

When \(T\) lies at or below the lower \(\alpha\) quantile of the central chi square distribution, no noncentrality is consistent with it at this level; the upper limit is then 0, as Yuan et al. (2016, Eq. 4) define the T-size RMSEA and as lavaan reports it, and the model is within tolerance for every positive bound. That happens with probability \(\alpha\) for a model that fits exactly and more often when the normal theory statistic is deflated, for example by data with light tails, so a statistic far below its degrees of freedom deserves a look at the data before it is read as evidence of fit.

Failing to reject \(H_0\) does not establish poor fit; it says only that fit within the bound has not been shown at this sample size. The test rests on the noncentral chi square approximation for a normal theory statistic. A scaled or robust statistic does not follow that distribution with this noncentrality, so it must not be supplied here; for a fitted model, including a robust (MLR, MLM), categorical (WLSMV), or FIML fit, sem_fit_measures reports this test as p_not_close_fit from lavaan's corrected measures. For a multiple group model the convention is Steiger's (1998): chisq, df, and N are totals over the groups, and the RMSEA and its limits carry the factor \(\sqrt{G}\).

References

Browne, M. W., & Cudeck, R. (1993). Alternative ways of assessing model fit. In K. A. Bollen & J. S. Long (Eds.), Testing structural equation models (pp. 136–162). Sage.

MacCallum, R. C., Browne, M. W., & Sugawara, H. M. (1996). Power analysis and determination of sample size for covariance structure modeling. Psychological Methods, 1(2), 130–149. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.1.2.130

Steiger, J. H. (1998). A note on multiple sample extensions of the RMSEA fit index. Structural Equation Modeling, 5(4), 411–419. doi:10.1080/10705519809540115

Steiger, J. H. (2000). Point estimation, hypothesis testing, and interval estimation using the RMSEA: Some comments and a reply to Hayduk and Glaser. Structural Equation Modeling, 7(2), 149–162.

Steiger, J. H., & Lind, J. C. (1980). Statistically-based tests for the number of common factors. Paper presented at the annual Spring meeting of the Psychometric Society, Iowa City, IA.

Yuan, K.-H., Chan, W., Marcoulides, G. A., & Bentler, P. M. (2016). Assessing structural equation models by equivalence testing with adjusted fit indexes. Structural Equation Modeling, 23(3), 319–330. doi:10.1080/10705511.2015.1065414

Examples

# Yuan et al. (2016, Example 1): nine holzinger_swineford
# tests in the Grant-White school (N = 145), the three-factor model with
# one cross-loading, T = 28.098 on 23 df. The 90 percent upper limit,
# their T-size RMSEA, is .083, so fit within .05 is not established.
equivalence_rmsea(chisq = 28.098, df = 23, N = 145, rmsea_bound = 0.05)
#>  term               value 
#>  rmsea              0.039 
#>  ci_lower           0.000 
#>  ci_upper           0.083 
#>  rmsea_bound        0.050 
#>  null_noncentrality 8.280 
#>  p_value            0.3906
#>  equivalent         0     
#>  chi_square         28.098
#>  df                 23    
#>  N                  145   
#>  n_groups           1     
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
#> 
#> Not close fit (RMSEA >= 0.05) is not rejected at alpha = 0.05: fit within the bound is not established (upper limit 0.0828), which is not evidence of poor fit.
#> Sample size: N = 145 in 1 group; multiplier a = 144 (sample_size_convention = "N-1")

# A bound of .09 is endorsed at alpha = .05.
equivalence_rmsea(chisq = 28.098, df = 23, N = 145, rmsea_bound = 0.09)
#>  term               value 
#>  rmsea              0.039 
#>  ci_lower           0.000 
#>  ci_upper           0.083 
#>  rmsea_bound        0.090 
#>  null_noncentrality 26.827
#>  p_value            0.0241
#>  equivalent         1     
#>  chi_square         28.098
#>  df                 23    
#>  N                  145   
#>  n_groups           1     
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
#> 
#> Not close fit (RMSEA >= 0.09) is rejected at alpha = 0.05: the population RMSEA is below the bound (upper limit 0.0828).
#> Sample size: N = 145 in 1 group; multiplier a = 144 (sample_size_convention = "N-1")

# The statistic lavaan reports for the two-school model of the same
# tests (formed with N, its default), with Steiger's (1998) multiple
# group convention.
equivalence_rmsea(chisq = 115.8513, df = 48, N = 301, rmsea_bound = 0.10,
                  n_groups = 2, sample_size_convention = "N")
#>  term               value  
#>  rmsea              0.097  
#>  ci_lower           0.075  
#>  ci_upper           0.120  
#>  rmsea_bound        0.100  
#>  null_noncentrality 72.240 
#>  p_value            0.4290 
#>  equivalent         0      
#>  chi_square         115.851
#>  df                 48     
#>  N                  301    
#>  n_groups           2      
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
#> 
#> Not close fit (RMSEA >= 0.1) is not rejected at alpha = 0.05: fit within the bound is not established (upper limit 0.12), which is not evidence of poor fit.
#> Sample size: N = 301 in 2 groups; multiplier a = 301 (sample_size_convention = "N")
